clinicalPearls: Cushing's: most clinical features (obesity, diabetes, diastolic hypertension, hirsutism, depression) are nonspecific; the more discriminatory signs are thinning/fragile skin with easy bruising, broad (>1 cm) purplish striae, and proximal myopathy (difficulty rising from a chair or climbing stairs). Suspect when several features cluster, or when a feature appears at an unusual age (e.g., osteoporosis in a young patient). (p.3056-3057)

Screen for endogenous Cushing's only after excluding exogenous (iatrogenic) glucocorticoids in any form. First-line screening tests: increased 24-h urinary free cortisol (three collections), failure to suppress morning cortisol after a 1 mg overnight dexamethasone test, and loss of diurnal rhythm shown by raised late-night (midnight) serum/salivary cortisol. Diagnosis is considered established when several tests are consistently abnormal. (p.3057)

Establish the diagnosis of Cushing's beyond doubt BEFORE doing any differential-diagnosis or imaging tests; most management errors (unnecessary imaging or surgery) come from not following this sequence, because pituitary and adrenal nodules are common incidental findings in the general population. (p.3057)

Cushing's differential diagnosis order: measure plasma ACTH first. Suppressed ACTH = ACTH-independent (adrenal) excess -> unenhanced adrenal CT. Normal/high ACTH = ACTH-dependent -> pituitary MRI plus dynamic tests (high-dose dexamethasone, CRH or desmopressin); pituitary MRI can be normal in up to 40% because microadenomas are small. (p.3057-3058)

Inferior petrosal sinus sampling (central:peripheral ACTH ratio >2 at baseline, >3 after CRH) distinguishes Cushing's disease from ectopic ACTH when dynamic tests are discordant; it cannot be used to lateralize the tumor within the pituitary, and no cortisol-lowering drugs should be used before it. (p.3058)

Primary aldosteronism is far more common than historically appreciated: prevalence 5-12% of hypertensives, higher in hypokalemic or drug-resistant hypertension. Screen only selected hypertensives (drug-resistant/severe hypertension, hypokalemia, adrenal mass, onset <40 years, or family history of primary aldosteronism), not all comers. (p.3060-3061)

Primary aldosteronism screen = aldosterone-renin ratio (ARR); correct hypokalemia first. Stop MR antagonists at least 4-6 weeks before testing; beta-blockers cause false positives and ACE inhibitors/ARBs cause false negatives. A positive ARR is followed by confirmatory testing (e.g., saline infusion test) by an endocrinologist. (p.3061)

After biochemical confirmation of aldosteronism, unenhanced adrenal CT plus adrenal vein sampling distinguish unilateral adenoma (Conn's, surgically curable by unilateral adrenalectomy) from bilateral hyperplasia (treated medically with an MR antagonist). AVS is only needed when surgery is feasible and desired. (p.3061)

Adrenal insufficiency: short cosyntropin (Synacthen) test is the safe, reliable first-line diagnostic test; failure is cortisol <450-500 nmol/L (16-18 microg/dL) at 30-60 min. Then measure plasma ACTH: high ACTH = primary (Addison's), inappropriately low ACTH = secondary/central. Increased plasma renin confirms mineralocorticoid deficiency in primary disease. (p.3068)

Primary adrenal insufficiency loses both glucocorticoid AND mineralocorticoid secretion; secondary (central) disease loses glucocorticoid only because the adrenal stays responsive to the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. Adrenal androgen secretion is lost in both. (p.3067)

Hyperpigmentation (palmar creases, friction/shear areas, sun-exposed skin) from excess POMC/ACTH is the hallmark distinguishing primary adrenal insufficiency; secondary insufficiency instead causes an alabaster-pale skin from ACTH lack. (p.3067)

Hyponatremia is present in ~80% of primary adrenal insufficiency at presentation and hyperkalemia in ~40%. Hyponatremia can also occur in secondary insufficiency via reduced cortisol inhibition of ADH (mild SIADH-like picture). (p.3067)

All patients with an incidentally discovered adrenal mass need a 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test to exclude cortisol excess; add plasma/urine metanephrines if HU >10 (exclude pheochromocytoma), and paired renin/aldosterone plus potassium if hypertensive. Confirm any Cushing's as ACTH-independent by measuring plasma ACTH. (p.3063-3064)

On unenhanced CT, adrenal lesion attenuation is the key discriminator: lipid-rich adenomas are typically <10-20 HU, whereas adrenocortical carcinoma and pheochromocytoma have high attenuation (>20 HU). Hounsfield assessment only applies to unenhanced CT, not post-contrast. (p.3064)

Mild autonomous cortisol secretion (MACS) = abnormal 1 mg dexamethasone test with no overt clinical Cushing's; it still carries excess risk of hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, osteoporosis, cardiovascular events, and mortality. A subset of primary aldosteronism patients have co-existing MACS ('Connshing' syndrome). (p.3061, p.3064)

CYP21A2 (21-hydroxylase) deficiency causes 90-95% of congenital adrenal hyperplasia; it impairs glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid synthesis and drives ACTH-mediated adrenal androgen excess. 17-hydroxyprogesterone is the diagnostic marker steroid. Severity spans classic salt-wasting (neonatal), simple virilizing, to nonclassic (presents in adolescence/adulthood). (p.3071)
harrison.pathophysiology: The adrenal cortex produces glucocorticoids (cortisol, zona fasciculata under HPA/ACTH control), mineralocorticoids (aldosterone, zona glomerulosa under renin-angiotensin-aldosterone control), and adrenal androgens. Cushing's syndrome reflects chronic glucocorticoid excess: ~90% of endogenous cases are ACTH-dependent (mostly a pituitary corticotrope adenoma = Cushing's disease, or ectopic ACTH from carcinoid/small-cell lung cancer), ~10% are ACTH-independent adrenal causes (adenoma, carcinoma, or bilateral macronodular/pigmented nodular hyperplasia). Cortisol excess upregulates gluconeogenesis, lipolysis, and protein catabolism, and when 11beta-HSD2 is overwhelmed cortisol activates the mineralocorticoid receptor, producing hypertension, hypokalemia, and edema. Primary mineralocorticoid excess (primary aldosteronism) is autonomous aldosterone production by the zona glomerulosa (bilateral hyperplasia or unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma/Conn's); MR over-activation causes sodium retention with volume expansion, potassium and hydrogen loss (hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis), and direct cardiac/renal damage. Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's) is destruction or dysfunction of the adrenal cortex (most often autoimmune adrenalitis, also TB, adrenoleukodystrophy, hemorrhage, infiltration, CAH), causing combined glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid deficiency; secondary insufficiency is HPA/pituitary-hypothalamic failure (tumor, surgery, irradiation, apoplexy/Sheehan's, or iatrogenic glucocorticoid suppression) with isolated glucocorticoid deficiency. CAH results from inherited steroidogenic enzyme defects (commonly CYP21A2) causing glucocorticoid deficiency, loss of feedback, raised ACTH, and adrenal androgen excess, with mineralocorticoid deficiency or excess depending on the enzymatic block.
additionalDifferentials: Cushing's disease (ACTH-producing pituitary corticotrope adenoma) vs ectopic ACTH syndrome (bronchial/pancreatic carcinoid, small-cell lung cancer, medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma)

ACTH-independent adrenal Cushing's: cortisol-producing adenoma, adrenocortical carcinoma, primary bilateral macronodular adrenal hyperplasia, primary pigmented nodular adrenal disease (Carney complex), McCune-Albright syndrome

Mineralocorticoid excess differential: bilateral micronodular hyperplasia vs unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma (Conn's); glucocorticoid-remediable aldosteronism (GRA/FH-I) and other familial primary aldosteronism; apparent mineralocorticoid excess (HSD11B2 deficiency); Liddle's syndrome (ENaC mutations); deoxycorticosterone excess from CAH (CYP11B1 or CYP17A1 deficiency)
Primary vs secondary (central) adrenal insufficiency, distinguished by plasma ACTH and renin
Pseudo-Cushing states: alcohol-related hypercortisolism, major depression, morbid obesity, and cyclic Cushing's
infectionMimics: Tuberculous adrenalitis (still a frequent cause of primary adrenal insufficiency in developing countries)
HIV-associated adrenal involvement (usually subclinical adrenal insufficiency)
Sepsis-associated bilateral adrenal hemorrhage (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome) causing acute primary adrenal insufficiency
Adrenal crisis presenting like an acute abdomen with fever, abdominal tenderness, nausea and vomiting
nonInfectiousMimics: Common population conditions overlapping Cushing's: obesity, type 2 diabetes, diastolic hypertension, hirsutism, depression, osteoporotic vertebral fractures
Pseudo-Cushing states (alcohol, major depression, morbid obesity)
Chronic adrenal insufficiency mistaken for depression or anorexia (nonspecific fatigue, weight loss)
Adrenal crisis mimicking acute abdomen or neurologic disease (stupor/coma)
Polycystic ovary syndrome phenotype mimicked by nonclassic CAH (hirsutism, oligomenorrhea)
Other causes of hypokalemic hypertension: licorice ingestion inhibiting 11beta-HSD2; renovascular/malignant hypertension (secondary hyperaldosteronism)
additionalInvestigations: Cushing's screening: 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test, late-night (midnight) salivary cortisol, 24-h urinary free cortisol (three collections); low-dose dexamethasone test if confirmation needed

Cushing's differential: plasma ACTH; pituitary MRI; high-dose dexamethasone test; CRH or desmopressin stimulation; bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling; unenhanced adrenal CT for ACTH-independent disease

Aldosteronism: aldosterone-renin ratio with serum potassium normalized; confirmatory saline infusion / oral sodium loading / fludrocortisone suppression test; unenhanced adrenal CT; adrenal vein sampling; 24-h urinary steroid profile (GC/MS) for familial/mimicking forms

Adrenal insufficiency: short cosyntropin (Synacthen/ACTH) stimulation test; plasma ACTH; plasma renin; adrenal steroid (21-hydroxylase) autoantibodies; insulin tolerance test as alternative; adrenal CT if autoantibody-negative; very-long-chain fatty acids in autoantibody-negative males (exclude X-ALD); pituitary MRI for secondary disease

Incidentaloma: 1 mg-DST in all; plasma/urine metanephrines if HU >10; paired renin and aldosterone plus potassium if hypertensive; 17-OHP, DHEAS, androstenedione (and sex steroids) if ACC suspected; unenhanced CT for size and attenuation (HU); chemical-shift MRI for indeterminate lesions

CAH: measurement of precursor steroids accumulating before the enzymatic block (notably 17-hydroxyprogesterone for 21-hydroxylase deficiency), preferably by mass spectrometry; androstenedione and testosterone for monitoring
redFlags: Adrenal crisis (acute adrenal insufficiency): postural hypotension progressing to hypovolemic shock, often after a prolonged period of nonspecific complaints; may mimic acute abdomen or neurologic decline (stupor/coma); can be triggered by intercurrent illness, surgery/stress, or increased glucocorticoid inactivation (e.g., hyperthyroidism) - treat immediately, do not let testing delay therapy
In suspected adrenal crisis, draw a baseline cortisol, start replacement, and defer formal stimulation testing - tests must never delay treatment
Cushing's hypercoagulable state with risk of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism
Acute paranoid or depressive psychosis in severe cortisol excess
Severe hypokalemia in aldosteronism causing arrhythmias, rhabdomyolysis, or hypokalemic paralysis; severe alkalosis causing tetany
Classic salt-wasting CAH in male neonates presenting as life-threatening adrenal crisis in the first weeks of life
harrison.prognosis: After successful removal of an ACTH- or cortisol-producing tumor the HPA axis remains suppressed and may take months to years (or never) to recover; recovery rates differ by cause - ectopic ACTH best (~80%, median ~7 months), Cushing's disease intermediate (~60%, ~17 months), adrenal Cushing's lowest (~40%, ~30 months). Even after cure, long-term quality of life can remain impaired with increased cardiovascular and osteoporotic-fracture risk depending on duration and degree of cortisol excess. Primary aldosteronism carries increased osteoporosis, type 2 diabetes, and cognitive dysfunction. Adrenal crisis is potentially lethal, with prospective data of 8.3 crises and 0.5 crisis-related deaths per 100 patient-years. MACS is associated with increased mortality. In CAH, fertility may be compromised (anovulation in women, testicular adrenal rest tumors and fibrosis in men).
pitfalls: Performing imaging or surgery before biochemically confirming Cushing's beyond doubt - pituitary/adrenal nodules are common incidental findings and lead to misdiagnosis
Forgetting to exclude exogenous (iatrogenic) glucocorticoid use as the cause before working up endogenous Cushing's

Dexamethasone test pitfalls: false non-suppression from oral estrogens/contraceptives (raise CBG/total cortisol; retest after 4-6 weeks off estrogen) and rapid dexamethasone inactivation by CYP3A4 inducers (antiepileptics, rifampicin); antibody-based urinary free cortisol assays have specificity problems improved by tandem mass spectrometry
Not normalizing potassium before, or failing to stop MR antagonists (4-6 weeks) before, ARR testing; beta-blockers give false-positive and ACE inhibitors/ARBs false-negative ARR results
Relying on the ARR alone when renin is very low increases false positives; only 10-40% of primary aldosteronism patients are hypokalemic, so normokalemia does not exclude it

Using random serum cortisol to diagnose adrenal insufficiency - baseline levels may be coincidentally low (diurnal rhythm), and secondary insufficiency often shows near-normal baseline cortisol that fails only on stimulation
Stopping exogenous glucocorticoids abruptly can precipitate iatrogenic adrenal insufficiency even though the patient still looks cushingoid

Judging adrenal mass attenuation on post-contrast CT - Hounsfield-unit discrimination of benign vs malignant only applies to unenhanced CT; lipid-poor adenomas (high HU) overlap with ACC and pheochromocytoma
Mistaking testicular adrenal rest tumors (TART) in CAH for testicular neoplasms
harrison.severityClassification: Adrenal insufficiency is classified as primary (Addison's, combined glucocorticoid + mineralocorticoid deficiency, high ACTH) vs secondary/central (isolated glucocorticoid deficiency, low/inappropriate ACTH), with acute adrenal crisis as the life-threatening acute form. Endogenous Cushing's is classified as ACTH-dependent (~90%; Cushing's disease vs ectopic ACTH) vs ACTH-independent (~10%; adenoma, carcinoma, hyperplasia). Cortisol excess severity ranges from overt Cushing's to mild autonomous cortisol secretion (MACS). Primary aldosteronism is divided into unilateral (adenoma/Conn's, surgically curable) vs bilateral (hyperplasia, medical therapy). CAH (21-hydroxylase deficiency) is graded by severity into classic salt-wasting, simple virilizing, and nonclassic forms. Adrenocortical carcinoma is staged by the ENSAT/TNM system (Stage I T1 <=5 cm to advanced/metastatic).
management: Treat endogenous Cushing's by removing the source, with transsphenoidal resection of a corticotroph adenoma or adrenalectomy for adrenal disease, using steroidogenesis inhibitors such as metyrapone or ketoconazole to control cortisol when surgery is delayed or incomplete
Manage primary aldosteronism with unilateral adrenalectomy for lateralising disease or a mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonist such as spironolactone or eplerenone for bilateral disease

Replace deficient hormones in adrenal insufficiency with glucocorticoid and, in primary disease, mineralocorticoid, and treat congenital adrenal hyperplasia with glucocorticoid to suppress adrenal androgen excess
Educate patients on sick-day rules, stress dosing and carriage of a steroid emergency card
Treat adrenal crisis urgently with parenteral hydrocortisone and intravenous fluid resuscitation
Monitor treatment response, HPA-axis recovery after tumour removal and complications, and screen selected hypertensives for primary aldosteronism
Coordinate care with endocrinology and endocrine surgery, offering genetic counselling in familial forms such as congenital adrenal hyperplasia
